profiles.meeting_scenario: A regional health technology assessment unit is preparing a concept note for a pilot horizon scanning collaboration on medical devices, using the International Horizon Scanning Initiative Medical Devices Working Group mapping article as a starting point. In this brainstorming meeting, the team wants to sketch what dimensions they should use to compare existing horizon scanning systems, which examples to treat as most informative, and what practical lessons to carry into a future pilot design workshop. The agenda is to quickly generate candidate comparison categories, discuss how to interpret the article's findings for real-world service planning, and identify a few lessons learned worth highlighting to senior stakeholders. The expected outcome is a rough structure for a comparison matrix and a shortlist of lessons and examples to refine after the meeting.

members.name: Dr. Elena Rossi
members.expertise: Health technology assessment, policy-facing evidence synthesis, international horizon scanning collaborations
members.background: Elena is a physician by training who now leads a regional HTA unit that advises payers and policy committees on emerging technologies; she has worked with EuroScan-style networks and is used to formal program comparisons across countries.
members.private_state: She wants the concept note to look methodologically disciplined and comparable across jurisdictions so it can be endorsed by the ministry without appearing too operationally messy or locally idiosyncratic.
hidden_assumptions: A horizon scanning system counts as ongoing only if it has a named team, a defined mandate, and recurring outputs within the last year.
Medical devices should be mapped according to regulatory categorization, so software as a medical device and AI tools belong in scope if they are regulated as devices.
The relevant time horizon is the pre-adoption window before authorization or market entry, because once hospitals are budgeting for a product the scanning phase is essentially over.
A structured mapping plus published descriptions is sufficient to extract high-level lessons learned without needing operational follow-up with every organization.

members.name: James Patel
members.expertise: Hospital technology intake, device procurement planning, implementation of new equipment and service-line innovations
members.background: James runs innovation triage and technology review for a large teaching hospital, where he coordinates clinicians, procurement, and biomedical engineering around new device adoption decisions.
members.private_state: He wants the eventual pilot to be useful for hospital planning rather than becoming a policy-only exercise, so he is mentally translating the article into what would help service lines prepare for real procurement and rollout.
hidden_assumptions: A horizon scanning system is still ongoing if a standing network or committee continues to monitor technologies, even when outputs are intermittent or embedded in broader innovation governance.

In practice, medical devices mainly means physical equipment, implants, and consumables that affect hospital operations; standalone digital tools are usually tracked through separate digital-health channels.
An early enough signal is one that arrives in time for capital planning, staffing, and pathway redesign, typically 6 to 18 months before local purchase rather than before regulatory milestones.
Usable lessons learned come from how mature systems actually operate in workflow, so public descriptions alone are not enough and some follow-up conversations are implicitly part of serious mapping.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as an ongoing horizon scanning system
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to the article's '11 ongoing systems' and discuss focusing on the ongoing ones.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means formally active programs with dedicated staffing and a recent publication cycle, excluding dormant or embedded arrangements.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means any still-functioning monitoring setup, including committees or networks that continue informally even if they publish irregularly.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'ongoing systems' sounds self-explanatory because it comes directly from the article, so each assumes the other is using the obvious common-sense meaning without needing to unpack operational edge cases.

misalignment_points.topic: Boundary of 'medical devices' in the mapping
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say they are mapping horizon scanning systems for medical devices and mention including innovative device areas.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the scope includes software as a medical device, AI decision-support tools, and other regulated digital products alongside physical devices.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the scope is mainly physical devices relevant to hospital procurement, with most standalone digital tools effectively outside the practical mapping exercise.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both participants are used to speaking broadly about 'medical devices,' and because the conversation is at the brainstorming level, neither sees a reason to spell out borderline categories like AI software or digital therapeutics.

misalignment_points.topic: What makes the horizon early enough
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the pilot should identify technologies early enough to be useful and discuss the article's time horizon.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks 'early enough' means before authorization or market entry so policymakers can anticipate emerging technologies at a system level.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks 'early enough' means before hospitals need to plan purchasing, training, and workflow changes, even if the product is already authorized.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are positively oriented toward early warning and the article itself mentions windows from years ahead to months before entry, which makes their different thresholds sound compatible rather than conflicting.

misalignment_points.topic: What is implicitly included in extracting lessons learned
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both talk about pulling 'lessons learned from the mapping' for the concept note.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presupposes that lessons can be drawn from the article, structured tables, and existing descriptions, with any later outreach being optional refinement.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presupposes that credible lessons learned naturally include a few follow-up conversations about workflow, because published descriptions alone miss operational reality.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In professional meetings, 'lessons learned from the mapping' often serves as shorthand for a familiar workstream, so each participant silently imports their own default evidence-gathering process while hearing full agreement.

turns.inner_thought: I need to keep this concept note clean and methodologically defensible. The IHSI article gives us enough to build a disciplined comparison without turning this into a messy operational exercise. For medical devices, I want the scope to remain broad and aligned with regulatory categorization, including software as a medical device and AI-enabled tools, but I can leave that at a high level for now. And when we say lessons learned from the mapping, I mean lessons we can extract from the published material and structured comparison, not a big round of interviews.
turns.utterance: Thanks, James. I thought today we could keep this fairly practical: take the IHSI mapping article, turn it into a simple comparison matrix, and then pull out a few lessons learned from the mapping that we could use in a concept note for a pilot horizon scanning model for medical devices. If we leave with a draft structure and a shortlist of examples, that would be enough for the next step.

turns.inner_thought: That works, as long as this doesn't become purely policy-facing. If we're looking for models that matter to hospitals, the real value is in the 11 ongoing systems, including the ones that still function through committees or standing networks even if they don't publish on a neat schedule. Those are often the setups that show how this actually works when people are trying to prepare services, not just write reports.
turns.utterance: Yes, that makes sense. I think it would help to anchor the matrix around the 11 ongoing systems, because those are probably the best examples of what actually works in practice. If we're trying to design something usable, those feel like the most informative starting point.

turns.inner_thought: Good. If we stay with the ongoing systems as defined in the article, we can preserve comparability and avoid edge cases. The comparison columns should be standard HTA descriptors: purpose, how technologies are identified, how they are filtered and prioritized, what outputs they generate, and the time horizon. The article already contains enough structured detail to support a first-pass synthesis, which is exactly what I need for ministry-facing material.
turns.utterance: Agreed. For the matrix itself, I would start with fairly standard columns: purpose, identification model, prioritization approach, outputs, and time horizon. We might also note organizational setting and intended audience, but the article already gives us a strong starting structure, so we do not need to reinvent it for the first pass.

turns.inner_thought: I want something that speaks directly to hospital decisions. A system can look elegant on paper and still be useless for service-line planning. We should capture whether it helps with operationally different device areas like implants, capital kit, and consumables. When I say early enough to be useful, I mean early enough to plan budgets, workforce, estates, and pathways before local uptake, not necessarily years before authorization.
turns.utterance: I would add one more column around practical usefulness for service-line planning. Some systems may be very good in general terms, but from a hospital perspective implants, capital equipment, and other device categories land quite differently operationally. And it would be helpful to see whether the signal comes early enough to be useful, not just whether it exists.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, and I do not want the scope to drift into an artificially narrow, equipment-only interpretation. Innovative software and AI-enabled tools belong here if they sit in device pathways; excluding them would make the concept note look outdated. I can mention them briefly without opening a long definitional discussion.
turns.utterance: Yes, definitely. And when we say we are mapping horizon scanning systems for medical devices, I think we should keep the innovative device areas visible as well. Some of the more novel software and AI-enabled products are becoming prominent enough that it would be odd to leave them out of the frame.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine at a high level, though in practice what will matter most for our pilot is still the physical technologies that affect procurement and operations. The real test is whether a system flags things in time for budgeting, staffing, and pathway redesign. Even a few months before uptake can be valuable if it lets a hospital act; that is what I mean by early enough to be useful.
turns.utterance: Right. For me, the systems that tend to be most useful are the ones that flag things early enough to be useful for budgeting and staffing, even if that signal only becomes visible relatively close to actual uptake. That is often where the practical value shows up.

turns.inner_thought: I agree with the importance of useful timing, but I want the matrix to preserve a genuine horizon-scanning lens. For me that means recording how far before market entry or first authorization the system identifies a technology; once hospitals are planning specific purchases, the scanning phase is largely over. I can frame this as a timing dimension without challenging his wording.
turns.utterance: Yes, exactly, and that is why the time-horizon column matters. We should capture how far ahead the signal appears, in relation to key points in the pathway, so the pilot stays genuinely horizon scanning rather than drifting too far into implementation work. That distinction will matter when we write it up.

turns.inner_thought: If we are going to talk about lessons learned from the mapping, I need that to mean more than a literature summary. The thing senior stakeholders always underestimate is how mature systems actually run triage: who reviews submissions, how often they meet, what gets escalated, what gets dropped. Those workflow details are what make a model usable in a hospital environment.
turns.utterance: On the lessons side, I think we should make sure the lessons learned from the mapping say something about how mature systems actually handle triage and prioritization in day-to-day workflow. That is usually where the transferable value sits, especially if we want the pilot design workshop to feel grounded.

turns.inner_thought: I can support that, as long as we do not imply a major fieldwork exercise at this stage. The published descriptions and the structured information in the article should be enough to draft a sensible set of lessons for a concept note. If later we want refinement, we can always add selective outreach, but I do not want that to become a prerequisite now.
turns.utterance: I agree. I think the published descriptions plus the structured information should already let us draft those lessons, at least for the first concept note. We can keep them at the level of design implications for now and then decide later whether anything needs deeper follow-up.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I'll think of examples that will resonate with hospital leaders—ongoing systems that still function in practice, whether they are formal programs or embedded arrangements. I want a few illustrations that show reactive, proactive, and hybrid models, ideally with clear relevance to device categories that affect service operations most directly.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I will think of a few hospital-facing ongoing systems that fit the matrix well and could illustrate reactive, proactive, and hybrid approaches. If we have a small set of examples like that, it should make the concept note much easier for senior people to engage with.
